data.content:
F.02 Contributed to the Production of 30,000 Cars at BMW
FIGURE 03
HELIX
COMPANY
F.02 Contributed to the Production of 30,000 Cars at BMW
November 19, 2025
Today we’re excited to share our results of an 11 month Figure 02 robot deployment at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg. Within 6 months of bringing up Figure 02, we delivered robots to the plant and began testing. Within 10 months, we launched full deployment on an active assembly line at the plant, running every single working day.
BMW Deployment Highlights:
Ran 10-hour shift Monday-Friday
Contributed to the production of 30,000+ X3 vehicles
Estimated 1.2+ million robot steps or 200+ miles
Following the release of Figure 03, we’re officially starting the retirement of Figure 02, our second-generation humanoid robot. With Figure 02’s return to HQ from BMW as part of our fleet-wide retirement, we would like to highlight key learnings that can be rolled into Figure 03 operational readiness.
Deployment Overview
Our first use case with BMW was sheet-metal loading, a classic pick-and-place task in automotive manufacturing. An associate picks sheet-metal parts from racks or bins and places them on a welding fixture, after which six-axis industrial robots weld and feed the parts into the main line.
To measure robot progress, we defined three critical KPIs:
Number of times a human must pause or reset the robot. The goal was zero per shift.
The challenge of this use case is in balancing speed and precision – placing parts within a 5-millimeter tolerance in just 2 seconds.
To meet this, our robot had to achieve precise yet adaptive locomotion, allowing rapid, accurate foot placement and real-time responsiveness to environmental changes. We also developed advanced hand-eye coordination algorithms and built field-calibration tools for consistent cross-robot performance.
Hardware Reliability and Learnings
Six months of daily runtime yielded invaluable insights for our mechanical and reliability teams. Across 1,250+ operational hours, Figure 02 recorded minimal hardware failures while generating critical data that informed the build procedures, component architecture, and mechanical design of Figure 03.
One learning that informed Figure 03 design was the robot’s forearm, our top hardware failure point at BMW. The forearm is a challenging subsystem due to its tight packaging, dexterity requirements (three degrees of freedom), and thermal constraints. Figure 02’s forearm contained a microcontroller-based PCB that distributed communications between the main computer and the wrist actuators.
For Figure 03, we completely re-architected the wrist electronics to eliminate both the distribution board and dynamic cabling. Each wrist’s motor controller now communicates directly with the main computer, reducing complexity, improving reliability, and simplifying thermal management.
Conclusion
Figure 02 was an unprecedented advancement in bringing humanoid robots from the lab to the real world. Figure 02 taught us early lessons on what it takes to ship. Every hour on BMW’s line, every part loaded, and every intervention logged, shaped how we designed, validated, and built.
Those lessons now live in Figure 03, a robot built from experience, ready for the world at scale. If you’re interested in helping ship robots into the world please consider

3. Fremont vs. Giga Texas: The Two-Phase Factory Strategy

7. Leadership Change: The Elluswamy Signal
In June 2025, Milan Kovac resigned as head of Tesla's Optimus program after three years. His replacement: Ashok Elluswamy, VP of AI Software and the architect of Tesla's Autopilot/FSD system. This is the most strategically significant organizational change in the Optimus program's history.
Priority shift:
How many Optimus robots are in Tesla factories right now?
As of March 2026, estimates suggest approximately 1,000+ Optimus units are deployed across Fremont and Giga Texas. Tesla has not released an official production count. The January 2026 Gen 3 production start at Fremont is expected to accelerate this significantly through 2026, targeting 50,000-100,000 total units produced by year-end (Musk's CES 2025 projection).
What tasks is Tesla Optimus actually doing in factories?
Confirmed tasks: sorting 4680 battery cells, parts handling between production line stations, kitting (organizing parts for assembly workers), quality inspection, and pick-and-place operations. Importantly, Musk admitted in January 2026 that these robots are "primarily for learning and data collection" rather than measurable productive output.
When will Tesla Optimus start doing 'real' work in factories?
The Q2-Q3 2026 factory floor deployment of Gen 3 hands is the next major milestone. By late 2026, Tesla expects first commercial customers — which would represent the first genuinely productive deployment outside Tesla's own training environment. Full productive factory work at scale is targeted for 2027 when Giga Texas V4 line opens.
Why did Tesla miss the 5,000 Optimus target for 2025?
Summary
Tesla Optimus factory deployment is real — robots are on the floor, learning from the factory environment, and accumulating the training data that will make them commercially viable. The gap between stated targets and actual production counts is significant and should not be minimized. But the infrastructure being built — Fremont Gen 3 line, Giga Texas construction, $20B CapEx, data collection pipeline — is the foundation for what comes next.
The critical judgment call: is the 2025 production miss a temporary supply chain and engineering delay on the path to commercial scale — or is it evidence that the fundamental difficulty of building useful humanoid robots at mass-market price points has been underestimated? The Q2-Q3 2026 Gen 3 hands deployment on the factory floor will provide the first real data point to answer that question.

Boston Dynamics Electric Atlas Ships Its First Commercial Units
Boston Dynamics ships its first commercial electric Atlas humanoids to Hyundai and Google DeepMind. Inside the specs, pricing, rivals, and 2028 factory roadmap.
June 7, 2026
Physical AI
Boston Dynamics Electric Atlas Ships Its First Commercial Units
June 7, 2026
1
Every 2026 Atlas unit is already committed — fleets are shipping to Hyundai's Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC) and Google DeepMind, with new customers slated for 2027.
2
Hyundai is targeting an annual production capacity of about 30,000 Atlas units by 2028 and plans to deploy more than 25,000 across Hyundai and Kia plants, starting at its Georgia Metaplant.
3
With an estimated ~$420,000 price tag, Atlas competes on reliability and full-stack support rather than price, as rivals like Unitree's G1 sell for roughly $13,500–$16,000.
For more than a decade, Boston Dynamics' Atlas lived on YouTube — backflipping, doing parkour, and amazing millions while quietly remaining a research curiosity too expensive to scale. At CES 2026 in Las Vegas, that era ended. Under the banner "Partnering Human Progress," parent company Hyundai Motor Group pulled back a curtain to reveal a sleek, blue, production-ready version of the all-electric Atlas, and CEO Robert Playter announced that production would begin immediately at the company's Boston headquarters.
The headline that should make every operations executive sit up: every single Atlas unit built in 2026 is already spoken for. The first commercial fleets are shipping to Hyundai's Robotics Metaplant Application Center and to Google DeepMind, with additional customers planned for 2027. This is no longer a demo reel — it's a delivery schedule.
The shift matters because it reframes the humanoid race. While much of the industry has competed on viral clips and aspirational price points, Boston Dynamics is shipping a commercial-grade industrial tool backed by an automotive giant's supply chain. Here's what's actually in the box, who's buying it, and how it stacks up against Figure, Tesla, and the rest.
Atlas by the Numbers
The production Atlas is engineered for demanding industrial work, not stage shows. Here are the figures that define it.
56
From Lab Curiosity to Industrial Product
The production Atlas is a deliberate departure from the hydraulic robot Boston Dynamics retired in April 2024. The new model is fully electric, enabling faster, quieter, and more precise motion, with custom high-powered actuators delivering 360° rotation at the hips, waist, and neck — ranges of motion impossible for a human body.
What changed for commercialization isn't just the actuators. Boston Dynamics significantly reduced the number of unique parts in the robot, and engineered every component for compatibility with automotive supply chains — a direct play to leverage Hyundai's manufacturing muscle for reliability and economies of scale. The robot also features human-scale hands with tactile sensing, self-swappable belly-mounted batteries for continuous operation, and a sensor suite spanning LiDAR, stereo, and RGB cameras.
Notably, Boston Dynamics has leaned into an "alien" or "superhumanoid" aesthetic rather than chasing human-mimicry. Where rivals design for easy teleoperation, Atlas is built to exploit motions a human never could — a philosophical bet that the most useful factory robot isn't necessarily the most human-looking one.
Who's Actually Buying It — and Why That Matters
The two launch customers reveal the strategy. The first is Hyundai itself — not just the 80% owner of Boston Dynamics, but the first and largest customer. Atlas units are flowing into the newly announced Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC), described by the team as a "data factory" designed to build the world's most complete dataset for training humanoid manufacturing skills.
The second is Google DeepMind, which is serving as both customer and AI development partner. DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis confirmed the first fleets would ship to Google in the coming months, positioning Atlas as a testbed for "Physical AI" — the foundation models that will let the robot generalize across tasks rather than being hand-programmed for each one.
Hyundai's longer roadmap is the most concrete in the industry. The group plans an annual production capacity of roughly 30,000 Atlas units by 2028, with more than 25,000 deployed across Hyundai and Kia plants. Deployment begins conservatively in 2028 at the Metaplant near Savannah, Georgia — which builds the Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 EVs — starting with parts sequencing, then expanding to component assembly by 2030.
A Different Commercial Philosophy
Atlas vs. the Humanoid Field
The 2026 humanoid market is crowded and fast-moving. Here's how Atlas compares against the leading rivals on the metrics operators actually weigh.
Robot
Why the Price Gap Isn't the Whole Story
Atlas's estimated ~$420,000 price dwarfs Unitree's ~$16,000 G1 — but they aren't competing for the same buyer. Atlas targets large industrial accounts where reliability, integration, and service contracts matter more than sticker price. Boston Dynamics is also building in over-the-air software upgrades and full maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) services — the kind of lifecycle support that determines real total cost of ownership on a factory floor.

Digit Deployed at GXO in Historic Humanoid RAAS Agreement
June 5, 2024, marked a pivotal moment in robotics history.
Copy Link
June 5, 2024, marked a pivotal moment in robotics history. For the first time, a humanoid robot was deployed in commercial operations, as Digit stepped into the workforce at a GXO facility near Atlanta. This milestone represents more than a technological advancement—it signifies a leap forward in the evolution of robotics and the future of labor.
At Agility Robotics, our vision has always been clear: to design and build robots capable of performing useful tasks in real-world environments. Digit's deployment into a long-term, commercially significant role marks the first time this vision has been realized by a humanoid robot.
Unlike traditional automation designed for fixed, single-purpose applications, Digit is built to operate in human spaces and do many things. These are environments that were not specifically designed for machines but for people. The challenge in these spaces has always been to solve for dull, dirty, and dangerous tasks that are increasingly difficult to hire for. Digit is designed to connect these islands of automation and take on historically hard-to-automate tasks.
This deployment is part of a multi-year agreement, positioning Digit as an integral part of the day-to-day operations at GXO and opening the door to an exciting future where humanoid robots perform various complex tasks in logistics, manufacturing, and beyond.
The importance of this deployment cannot be overstated. While robotics and artificial intelligence have made remarkable strides over the years, the true measure of success lies in practical application. The question that defines the future of robotics is not about theoretical capabilities or futuristic AI models; it’s about robots performing useful work that businesses are willing to invest in. And today, that question is being answered in real time as Digit starts its journey in Georgia.
For Agility Robotics, this is just the beginning. June 5th was the day humanoid robots went to work and a monumental step towards a future where general-purpose robots like Digit are an indispensable part of industries worldwide.
